A display of polar stratospheric clouds (also called nacreous or mother-of-pearl clouds) was seen from Ireland this morning prior to, and just at, sunrise. This pic is from the daughter of one of the IAS members in Dublin. They had appeared the last couple of days from Norway and Scotland but are now pushing a little further south. The season for them is usually from January but they have been unusually early this year. Temperatures in the stratosphere need to be below -85 Celsius for them to form. I have seen them once before in 2015 but keep an eye out the next few mornings if clear. spaceweather.com has added a sightings alert to their page via a graphic showing temperatures in the stratosphere.

One for John F.    Amateur astronomer Piqui Diaz, of Ezeiza, Argentina, 'discovered' this clair-obscur effect that caught her eye while observing the Moon with her 90mm refractor in early 2023, a feature she since dubbed Piqui's Scissors. It's a remarkably realistic-looking pair of closed scissors visible near the terminator when the Moon is five or six days old. The paired craters Atlas and Hercules form the finger holes with Keldysh at the blades' pivot point. A string of hilly terrain extends in a broken line to the north and traces the tool's closed blades.  Strange no-one saw it before, or at least did but never noted it in the literature? o

There’s a new comet headed into the inner solar system! Now officially named C/2026 A1 (MAPS), it’s the 1st comet discovered in 2026. It’s a sungrazing comet, possibly a member of the Kreutz family of comets, and it will make its extremely close pass by the sun on April 4-5. C/2026 A1 (MAPS) might be as large as 2.4 km across, and could be a chunk from an even larger comet.  In March we might be able to pick it up in Cetus.

China might yet beat US to Moon - On Feb 11th, CMSA completed a major test of its Long March-10 rocket and the Mengzhou spacecraft.  The test took place at the Wenchang Spacecraft Launch Site in south China's Hainan Province.  I spent a week touring around Hainan Island in 2007, but was not allowed anywhere near the then fledgling facility, (obviously).  If I recall correctly, the launch site was finished around 2013/4, somewhat a long time for the Chinese - I have witnessed first hand an entire manufacturing industrial estate at least the size of Shannon, with many fully operative companies (including one I was to be based in) along with a 11 km stretch of 4-lane motorway being built alongside in just 3 weeks from date of first breaking ground!! I lived in China for several months and that construction rate was surreal. And, the building quality I have to say was top class.  Granted they can throw a literal army of labourers at it, but still, very impressive.  Image shows the rocket after dropping boosters

Another potential naked eye comet?  One week after the full moon in April, Comet C/2025 R3 Panstarrs is expected to become visible without optical aid. On March 23, it reached a mag 7.8 for the first time, and its brightness has increased significantly in recent weeks. It will not reach its perihelion, nor its closest approach to Earth, for another month.  One for Angela to include in Apr Sky at Night?

A very impressive photo by Michael Murphy of the IAS in Dublin that shows the big spot group now rounding the Sun’s limb.   I could see AR 4475 and AR 4478 with my 6x30mm Sunoculars earlier this morning. The latter region showed bright faculae despite the group still just sitting on the Sun’s edge. Perhaps limb darkening allowed the faculae to stand out more in these instruments.  See https://spaceweather.com also.
